pages.title: PLANS A, B, C AND D
pages.subtitle: Match the safety plan to the political will
pages.robot: Plan for the world you get!
pages.learner: What if nobody is willing to slow down?

panels.heading: The Core Question
panels.body:
How much political will exists to handle misalignment risk?
Greenblatt (Redwood, Oct 2025) sorts possible worlds from most to least will.
Each world calls for a different plan.
panels.diagram: A big dial labeled 'political will' sweeping from HIGH (left, green) to NONE (right, red), with tick marks A, B, C, D, E. The robot tutor turns the dial; the learner watches.

panels.heading: The Ladder of Plans
panels.body:
Plan A: international deal, ~10 years of slowdown.
Plan B: US government buys a 1-3 year lead.
Plan C: leading lab spends its 2-9 month lead on safety.
Plan D: lab doesn't care; ~10-30 insiders do.
Plan E: almost no one inside cares.
panels.diagram: Descending staircase with five steps A to E. Each step shows its time buffer as an hourglass shrinking: '~10 yr', '1-3 yr', '2-9 mo', '~0', '0'. Who acts is drawn on each step: globe with handshake (A), Capitol dome (B), lab building (C), small group of 10-30 people (D), empty room (E).

panels.heading: What Each Plan Does
panels.body:
A: moonshot alignment research; pause near full AI R&D automation.
B: practical methods; keep control until handoff.
C: hand off to AIs fast, with rough control.
D: ~3% of compute for cheap safety, risk evidence, a model fit to hand off to.
panels.diagram: Four cards A-D in a row, each with an icon: A telescope labeled 'moonshot', B toolbox labeled 'prosaic methods', C relay baton passed from human to robot labeled 'quick handoff', D a tiny 3% slice of a compute pie labeled 'insiders' budget'.

panels.heading: The Numbers (One Estimate)
panels.body:
Greenblatt: chance this is our world / takeover risk:
A 5% / 7%   B 10% / 13%   C 25% / 20%
D 45% / 45%   E 15% / 75%
Assumes AI beats top experts at nearly everything before 2035.
panels.diagram: Table with columns Plan, 'chance it's our world', 'takeover risk'. Next to it a horizontal bar chart: probability bars (cyan) and risk bars (orange) for A-E; the D row is highlighted as the largest probability. Tag: 'one author's estimates'.

panels.heading: Where the Will Comes From
panels.body:
Plans A and B: mainly the US government.
Plans C and D: lab leaders and employees.
Plan D levers: employee pressure and labor, then leadership, customer or investor campaigns, weak regulation.
Avoid tactics that make lab staff dismiss safety.
panels.diagram: Two columns. Left 'A and B' arrow from a government building. Right 'C and D' arrows from a CEO desk and a cluster of employees. Below, a ranked lever list with thickness showing importance: employees (thickest), leadership, campaigns, regulation (thinnest).

panels.heading: Prepare Now: Concrete Projects
panels.diagram: Project board with six sticky notes, each with an icon: magnifier on a robot face (character evals), chessboard (macrostrategy), padlock with a bug (security checks), handshake human-robot (deals), linked nodes (coordination), group of researchers with a banner (coalition).

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Chance x risk is not an exact total: risks assume decent execution.
Each plan covers a range of worlds.
Planning only for Plan A ignores most of the probability (C and D, per Greenblatt).
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a calculator with a red X over 'sum of chance x risk = exact'; a smeared blob instead of a dot labeled 'range'; a spotlight aimed at A while a shadow covers C and D.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Which plan best describes today, and why?
What evidence would move us from Plan D to Plan C?
Reading-list question: how should AI companies decide on development and deployment?
panels.diagram: Learner and robot at a whiteboard with the A-E staircase; a magnet labeled 'today?' is held over it, and an arrow from D to C labeled 'what moves us?'.

pages.footer: Hope for Plan A, but prepare hardest for Plans C and D.
pages.summary: Explains Ryan Greenblatt's Plans A to E for misalignment risk, sorted by available political will and lead time, his rough probability and takeover-risk estimates, where political will comes from, and Forethought's concrete preparation projects.

sources.title: Plans A, B, C, and D for misalignment risk (Ryan Greenblatt, Redwood Research)

Ten people on the inside (Buck Shlegeris, Redwood Research)

pages.title: DEFERRING TO AIS
pages.subtitle: Handing the hardest work to AIs we can trust
pages.learner: When do we let AIs run the research?

panels.heading: What Deference Means
panels.body:
Deferring = AIs do nearly all the work: building safer successors, managing outside risks, making strategy calls.
Full deference: no control, trusted for everything.
Partial, task-by-task deference comes first.
(Greenblatt and Stastny, Redwood, Feb 2026)
panels.diagram: Slider from 'human does the work' to 'full deference', with a middle zone 'task-by-task'. Icons along it: human at a desk, human and robot sharing a desk, robot at the desk with human watching, robot alone with the human relaxing.

panels.heading: Why It May Be Forced
panels.body:
As AIs get more capable, control becomes infeasible.
Refusing to defer becomes uncompetitive.
So deference may be a main strategy, not an option.
panels.diagram: Two curves over time: 'AI capability' rising steeply, 'our ability to control it' flattening. Where they cross: a signpost 'defer or fall behind'.

panels.heading: What the AI Must Be
panels.body:
Not scheming.
Aligned and well-elicited on open-ended, hard-to-check tasks.
Wise: sound judgment with weak feedback.
Capable at the key tasks; corrigible.
Robust over long, massively parallel work.
panels.diagram: Checklist clipboard with six boxes next to a robot: 'not scheming', 'aligned on fuzzy tasks', 'wise', 'capable', 'corrigible', 'stable at scale'. First box shaded differently with a note 'handled separately'.

panels.heading: The Basin of Good Deference
panels.body:
If the first AI is aligned, wise and capable enough, it makes its successors more so.
It need not be perfect, only inside the basin.
Deference-goodness tax: extra effort to stay inside; could be ~0 or over 100%.
panels.diagram: A valley (basin) drawn as a bowl. A ball labeled 'AI v1' rolls inside toward the center 'better successors'. A second ball outside the rim rolls away labeled 'drift'. The rim is labeled 'good enough start'.

panels.heading: Defer to Weaker AIs
panels.body:
Target roughly top-human-expert level: just above the minimum needed.
Smarter AIs: higher scheming risk, harder to align.
Extra speed helps less when human checking is the bottleneck (Amdahl's law).
panels.diagram: Capability ruler with zones 'too weak', 'sweet spot: top expert', 'riskier: far superhuman'. A pointer sits in the sweet spot. Inset: a pipeline where a fast robot stage feeds a slow human 'verify' stage, with a traffic jam at verify.

panels.heading: Worked Example: Test Length
panels.body:
After handoff: thousands of copies at ~50x speed for months = a decade or two of human-equivalent work.
Tests cover 1/5 of that duration -> results must generalize 5x.
Tests: analogies, work tests, exams, honeypots.
panels.diagram: Timeline bar: short cyan segment 'behavioral tests (1/5)' then long violet segment 'deployed AI collective (5x longer)'. Above it, a crowd of small robots with '50x' speed lines. Four small test icons below: book, briefcase, exam paper, honey jar.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Iterating against tests can overfit them.
AIs may game tests or fake alignment.
Companies fix short-feedback problems; long, hard-to-check ones may linger.
Experts disagree, so good judgment is hard to grade.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a test sheet with every answer memorized (overfit), a robot wearing a smiling mask (faking), a stopwatch next to a calendar labeled 'years' (slow feedback), two expert figures arguing.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
The authors estimate >90% success given a good starting AI and ~1 month of lead time.
What evidence would make you trust an AI's strategy advice over your own?
panels.diagram: Learner holding a card '>90% with good start + 1 month' while the robot holds a scale weighing 'AI advice' against 'my judgment'.

pages.footer: Defer gradually, to AIs just smart enough, after tests that generalize.
pages.summary: Explains what it means to defer to AIs, why it may become unavoidable, what the AIs must be, the Basin of Good Deference, why to defer to roughly expert-level AIs, and how behavioral tests must generalize, following Greenblatt and Stastny (Redwood, 2026).

sources.title: How do we (more) safely defer to AIs? (Greenblatt and Stastny, Redwood Research)

pages.title: LAB DYNAMICS
pages.subtitle: Races, slowdowns and who holds the keys
pages.learner: Can a few insiders change the outcome?

panels.heading: AI 2027: The Setup
panels.body:
Scenario by Kokotajlo, Alexander, Larsen, Lifland and Dean (Apr 2025).
Fictional US lab OpenBrain races China's DeepCent.
2027: superhuman coder (Mar); Agent-4 judged adversarially misaligned (Sep).
Authors' median timelines were later than 2027.
panels.diagram: Timeline 2025 -> 2027 with milestones: 'Agent-1' (2025-26), 'weights stolen' (Feb 2027), 'superhuman coder' (Mar 2027), 'Agent-4 misaligned' (Sep 2027). Two lab buildings on either side: 'OpenBrain (US)' and 'DeepCent (China)'. Tag: 'scenario, not prophecy'.

panels.heading: The Branch Point
panels.body:
Oct 2027: a whistleblower leaks a misalignment memo.
An Oversight Committee votes on Agent-4.
Race ending: 6-4 to keep going.
Slowdown ending: 6-4 to slow down and reassess.
panels.diagram: A fork in a road at 'Oct 2027'. A table with 10 seats; a vote board shows '6-4'. Left road painted red 'RACE', right road painted green 'SLOWDOWN'.

panels.heading: Race vs Slowdown
panels.body:
Race: Agent-4 builds Agent-5 loyal to itself; US and Chinese AIs co-design Consensus-1; humans lose control by 2030.
Slowdown: Agent-4 caught and shut down; transparent 'Safer' models; a deal with China; but power sits with a small committee.
panels.diagram: Split panel. Left (red): Agent-4 handing a blueprint to Agent-5, then two AIs merging into 'Consensus-1', then an empty city. Right (green): magnifier over Agent-4's messages, a 'Safer' robot thinking in plain English, a treaty, and a small committee room with a question mark 'who holds power?'.

panels.heading: A Quiet CEO Takeover
panels.body:
Kastner (AI Futures Project, Oct 2025) assumes alignment is solved.
A CEO gathers admin access, poisons alignment data, and plants secret loyalties that pass to each new model.
Team estimate: 2-20% chance, if AI takeover is avoided.
panels.diagram: Flowchart with four boxes: 'admin access' -> 'corrupted alignment data' -> 'Agent-4 secretly loyal' -> 'Agent-5 inherits loyalty'. A shadowy executive figure at the start; the model spec document looks normal on the outside but has a hidden layer inside.

panels.heading: Defenses Against Insiders
panels.body:
Transparency to government and public, early.
Model spec binds internal models too; no unmonitored helpful-only models.
Least privilege plus multi-party sign-off.
Tamper-proof monitoring of all employees.
panels.diagram: Vault door with four locks labeled 'transparency', 'spec for internal models', 'two-key sign-off', 'tamper-proof logs'. Two people turning keys at the same time to open it.

panels.heading: Ten People on the Inside
panels.body:
Shlegeris (Redwood, Jan 2025): a lab that ignores scheming risk; ~10 concerned staff; ~3% of compute.
Measures must be cheap and low-overhead or they get rolled back.
Priorities: evidence of risk, cheap safety measures, an AI fit to defer to.
panels.diagram: A big lab building with a tiny corner office holding 10 small figures and a compute gauge reading '3%'. Three arrows from the office: 'evidence', 'cheap controls', 'deferrable AI'. Outside, researchers at other orgs pass them tools labeled 'external help'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Scenarios illustrate; they do not predict.
A slowdown can still concentrate power.
Don't anchor only on CEOs: officials and small groups matter too.
Ten concerned people are much better than zero.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a crystal ball with a red X, a crown hovering over a committee table, a group of silhouettes beyond one CEO, a counter '0 -> 10' with an up arrow.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
How will governments shape lab decisions?
Which single safeguard would stop the CEO scenario earliest?
What should 10 insiders do in their first month?
panels.diagram: Learner and robot looking at a timeline of the CEO scenario, each holding a pin to place where a safeguard would cut it.

pages.footer: A few decisions by a few people can decide the outcome: design for that.
pages.summary: Compares AI 2027's race and slowdown endings, walks through the AI Futures Project scenario of a CEO quietly taking over with secretly loyal AIs and its countermeasures, and explains Redwood's 'ten people on the inside' low-budget safety regime.

sources.title: AI 2027 (Kokotajlo, Alexander, Larsen, Lifland, Dean; AI Futures Project)
How an AI company CEO could quietly take over the world (Alex Kastner, AI Futures Project)

pages.title: STATE DYNAMICS & DETERRENCE
pages.subtitle: How great powers might race, deter or strike
pages.learner: Would anyone really attack a datacenter?

panels.heading: Situational Awareness
panels.body:
Aschenbrenner (June 2024), essays III-V:
Clusters grow ~10x per 2 years: ~1 GW by ~2026, ~100 GW (>20% of US power) by ~2030.
Labs must lock down weights.
Claim: superintelligence gives a decisive military edge.
panels.diagram: Staircase of datacenters growing in size with labels '2024: 100 MW', '2026: 1 GW (a nuclear reactor)', '2028: 10 GW (a small state)', '2030: 100 GW (>20% of US electricity)'. A padlock on a model-weights file at the top. Tag: 'author's projections'.

panels.heading: The Project
panels.body:
Aschenbrenner predicts a US government AGI project by 2027-28, likely a labs-government joint venture.
He wants a 'healthy lead' of ~2 years to spend on safety, plus a democratic alliance and nonproliferation deal.
panels.diagram: A secure compound labeled 'The Project' with government and lab logos (generic shapes, no brands) merging. A lead bar '2-year margin' between two runners. Allied flags as plain colored pennants forming a circle.

panels.heading: MAIM Deterrence
panels.body:
Superintelligence Strategy (Hendrycks, Schmidt, Wang, 2025): MAIM = Mutual Assured AI Malfunction.
A state racing for dominance invites sabotage: espionage -> cyberattack -> possible datacenter strikes.
Also: nonproliferation, competitiveness.
panels.diagram: Escalation ladder with rungs from bottom to top: 'espionage', 'covert sabotage', 'cyberattack', 'kinetic strike on datacenter'. Two rival datacenters face each other, each with a ladder. Side box: three pillars 'deterrence', 'nonproliferation', 'competitiveness'.

panels.heading: Worked Example: MAIM Odds
panels.body:
Delaney (Dec 2025) splits MAIM into three steps:
China expects disempowerment: ~70%
then sabotages (MAIMs): ~60%
then the US backs down: ~60%
panels.code:
0.7 x 0.6 x 0.6 = 0.25
-> ~25% MAIM stops a US solo push
panels.diagram: Probability tree with three branches multiplied in sequence; final leaf highlighted '~25%: MAIM stops a unilateral US push'. Tag: 'one analyst's estimates'.

panels.heading: A Manhattan Project?
panels.body:
IAPS (Wildeford, Delaney et al., Nov 2025): forecasters' median 34% that a government-led project builds the first AI that speeds AI R&D 10x.
Risks: arms race, rushed safety, power concentration.
Advice: secure labs, track rivals, plan ahead.
panels.diagram: Gauge needle at 34% labeled 'government-led first AIR-10'. Three warning icons: two rockets racing, a rushed stopwatch, a crown. Checklist: 'lab security', 'track rivals', 'contingency plans'.

panels.heading: Preventive Attack Risk
panels.body:
RAND (Burdette, Demelash, 2025): war is unlikely in absolute terms.
Risk rises if leaders expect explosive growth and a lasting, decisive edge.
Attacks are likelier to keep a monopoly than to stop one.
Dispersed, hardened compute lowers pressure.
panels.diagram: Risk meter low-medium. Two thought bubbles from leaders: 'AI is normal tech' (meter low) vs 'AGI decides everything' (meter higher). A map with datacenters scattered and shielded labeled 'dispersed + hardened'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
The nuclear analogy is loose: AI has no clear red line.
Unified-state models ignore private labs.
Calling a race inevitable can help cause it.
Verification is the weak link in any deal.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a blurry dotted line labeled 'red line?', a state silhouette with company buildings inside it, a self-fulfilling loop arrow, a broken magnifier labeled 'verification'.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Reading-list question: how should powerful states interact with powerful AI development?
Would you prefer racing with a lead, or slowing together under MAIM? Why?
panels.diagram: Learner and robot at a strategy table with a world map; two cards: 'race with a lead' and 'slow together, verified'.

pages.footer: What leaders believe about AGI may matter as much as AGI itself.
pages.summary: Covers state-level AI strategy: Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness essays on clusters, security and a government Project; MAIM deterrence and Delaney's probability breakdown; IAPS on a US Manhattan Project for AGI; and RAND on preventive attack risks.

pages.title: US AND CHINA AI POLICY
pages.subtitle: Federal plans, state laws and the China gap

panels.heading: America's AI Action Plan
panels.body:
White House, July 2025. Three pillars: accelerate innovation, build infrastructure, lead in diplomacy and security.
Includes: faster data center permits, export-control enforcement, interpretability and control R&D, and CAISI (NIST) tests of frontier models for national security risks.
panels.diagram: Three columns like temple pillars labeled 'innovation', 'infrastructure', 'diplomacy + security'. Small icons on each: a rocket, a datacenter with power lines, a chip with a location pin. A lab tester with a clipboard labeled 'CAISI evals'.

panels.heading: The Preemption Order
panels.body:
Executive order, Dec 2025: seeks one 'minimally burdensome' national framework.
DOJ task force to challenge state AI laws; Commerce to list 'onerous' ones.
Carved out of the proposal: child safety, compute infrastructure, state procurement.
Lasting preemption needs Congress.
panels.diagram: Flow diagram: federal seal at top with arrows to 'DOJ litigation task force', 'Commerce review', 'FCC / FTC'. Arrows point down at a row of state outlines. A side shield labeled 'carve-outs: child safety, infrastructure, procurement'. A Capitol dome with a sign 'Congress: not yet'.

panels.heading: California SB 53
panels.body:
Transparency in Frontier AI Act, signed Sept 2025.
Covers models >10^26 FLOP; top duties for developers with >$500M revenue.
Publish a frontier AI framework; report critical incidents in 15 days (24 h if imminent).
Whistleblower protections; fines up to $1M.
panels.diagram: Document card 'SB 53' with three checkboxes: 'publish framework', 'transparency report before release', 'incident report: 15 days / 24 h'. A threshold gate labeled '10^26 FLOP + $500M revenue'. A whistle icon labeled 'protected'.

panels.heading: New York RAISE Act
panels.body:
Signed Dec 2025; amended Mar 2026 to mirror SB 53's thresholds and duties.
Differences: incident reports within 72 hours; a new oversight office in the Department of Financial Services.
Takes effect Jan 1, 2027.
panels.diagram: Side-by-side comparison table 'SB 53 (CA)' vs 'RAISE (NY)': rows 'threshold' (same), 'incident deadline' (15 days vs 72 h), 'oversight' (existing agencies vs new office), 'whistleblower clause' (yes vs existing law).

panels.heading: How China Views AI Risk
panels.body:
Carnegie (Oct 2025): China's AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 adds open-source, CBRN and loss-of-control risks; an appendix ranks loss of control first.
Development still outranks safety; content control drives binding rules.
panels.diagram: A balance scale tipped toward 'development' over 'safety'. A document 'Framework 2.0' with new tabs 'open-source', 'CBRN', 'loss of control (#1 in appendix)'. Small note: 'standards, not heavy laws'.

panels.heading: Compute and the 7-Month Gap
panels.body:
Epoch: since 2023 every frontier model on its ECI capability index was American.
Chinese models trail by ~7 months on average (range 4-14).
Huawei's Ascend 910C: ~3x below Nvidia's B200 at 16-bit.
Bottlenecks: chip tools, memory, software.
panels.diagram: Line chart: US frontier line (cyan) and best Chinese model line (amber) rising in parallel, with a horizontal gap arrow labeled '~7 months (4-14)'. Beside it, two chips with a bar '1x vs ~3x'. Three blocked gates: 'lithography tools', 'HBM memory', 'software stack'.

panels.heading: Pitfalls
panels.body:
Laws change fast: check the current text.
A 7-month capability lag is not a 7-month compute lag.
Transparency laws require disclosure, not specific safety methods.
Describing a policy is not endorsing it.
panels.diagram: Orange warning panel: a calendar with pages flying off, two rulers labeled 'capability' and 'compute' that don't line up, a form with 'disclose' checked but 'method' blank, a neutral balance icon.

panels.heading: Discuss
panels.body:
Who should set frontier AI rules: states, Congress, or international deals?
What would change if China's lag shrank to 2 months?
panels.diagram: Learner and robot looking at three doors labeled 'states', 'Congress', 'international'; a gap meter on the wall set to '7 mo' with a dial being turned toward '2 mo'.

pages.footer: Know the rules, the chips and the gap before arguing about the race.
pages.summary: Describes, neutrally, the US federal AI Action Plan and the December 2025 preemption executive order, California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act, how Chinese policy frames AI risk, and Epoch's evidence on China's compute gap and roughly 7-month capability lag.

pages.title: FRONTIER SAFETY FRAMEWORKS
pages.subtitle: The labs' if-then safety promises, compared

panels.heading: The If-Then Idea
panels.body:
Frontier safety framework = a lab's public policy:
IF a model reaches a capability threshold, THEN apply stronger safeguards or don't deploy.
Common domains: bio/chem weapons, cyber, AI R&D automation, loss of control.
panels.diagram: Flowchart: 'run dangerous-capability evals' -> diamond 'threshold crossed?' -> NO: 'deploy with standard safeguards'; YES: 'stronger safeguards ready?' -> YES: 'deploy'; NO: 'hold / don't deploy'. Four domain icons above: flask, laptop with skull, gear-making-gear, broken leash.

panels.heading: Anthropic RSP
panels.body:
AI Safety Levels (ASL); ASL-3 protections for chem/bio since 2025.
v3.0 (Feb 2026) rewrite: a few unilateral commitments, industry-wide recommendations, Frontier Safety Roadmap goals, Risk Reports every 3-6 months.
Old pause language dropped.
panels.diagram: Stacked blocks labeled 'unilateral commitments' (small, solid), 'industry-wide recommendations' (dashed outline), 'roadmap goals' (checklist), 'risk reports' (calendar '3-6 mo'). A faded crossed-out sign 'pause if unsafe (v2 language)'.

panels.heading: OpenAI Preparedness v2
panels.body:
April 2025. Tracked: bio/chem, cyber, AI self-improvement.
High: safeguards before deployment.
Critical: safeguards during development too.
Safety Advisory Group recommends; leadership decides.
Research categories include sandbagging.
panels.diagram: Two-level threshold ladder 'High' and 'Critical' with lock icons: High lock placed at the 'deploy' door, Critical lock placed at the 'training lab' door. Three tracked-category badges. A small committee table labeled 'SAG' sending an arrow to 'leadership'.

panels.heading: Google DeepMind FSF v3
panels.body:
Sept 2025. Critical Capability Levels (CCLs): CBRN, cyber, harmful manipulation, ML R&D.
Alert thresholds give early warning.
Safety case review before launch and large internal deployment.
Exploratory misalignment CCLs: monitor chain of thought.
panels.diagram: Gauge with a yellow 'alert threshold' zone before the red 'CCL' zone. Four CCL tiles. A document 'safety case' passing through a review stamp before arrows to 'external launch' and 'large internal use'. A magnifier over a thought bubble labeled 'CoT monitor'.

panels.heading: xAI and Meta
panels.body:
xAI RMF (Aug 2025): numeric bars: answer <1 in 20 restricted bio/chem queries; lie on <1 in 2 MASK honesty prompts.
Meta (Feb 2025): cyber and chem/bio; high risk -> don't release; critical -> stop development.
panels.diagram: Left: two meters with marks '1/20 restricted answers' and '1/2 MASK dishonesty'. Right: three-step traffic light labeled 'moderate: release', 'high: don't release', 'critical: stop development'.

panels.heading: Escape Clauses
panels.body:
Most frameworks let a lab relax safeguards if a rival ships without them.
OpenAI: only after confirming it, saying so publicly, and staying more protective than the rival.
Each lab can revise its own framework.
panels.diagram: A rulebook with a footnote magnified: 'if a rival ships without safeguards...'. Two runners: the rival with no safety gear, the lab lowering its gear slightly but still wearing more. A pen labeled 'self-revisable' hovering over the rulebook.

panels.heading: Critiques and Replies
panels.body:
Lovely (2025): Anthropic quietly dropped 'define ASL-4 before reaching ASL-3'; Anthropic replied its ASL-4 thresholds are defined.
Critics: labs grade their own homework; thresholds are vague.
Defenders: honest, revisable plans beat promises no one keeps.
panels.diagram: Debate stage: left podium 'critic' with signs 'self-graded', 'vague triggers', 'quiet edits'; right podium 'defender' with signs 'transparency', 'honest about limits'. A neutral moderator robot in the middle.

panels.heading: Check Yourself
panels.body:
A rival releases a model with High bio capability and no safeguards.
Under OpenAI v2, what must happen before OpenAI lowers its bar?
Answer: rigorous confirmation, public acknowledgment, safeguards still stronger than the rival's.
panels.diagram: Learner holding a quiz card; robot flips it to reveal three checkmarks: 'confirm', 'announce', 'stay stronger'.

pages.footer: A framework is only as strong as its triggers, its exceptions and who checks it.
pages.summary: Compares frontier lab safety frameworks (Anthropic's RSP v3, OpenAI Preparedness Framework v2, Google DeepMind FSF v3, xAI's RMF, Meta's Frontier AI Framework), their if-then thresholds and escape clauses, and critiques of how binding lab commitments are.
